items._ogDesc: As Canada looks to develop closer economic ties with the European Union (EU), a new report suggests there is billions of dollars’ worth of untapped demand for Canadian goods and services in Europe.
items.body:
As Canada looks to develop closer economic ties with the European Union (EU), a new report suggests there is billions of dollars’ worth of untapped demand for Canadian goods and services in Europe.

The report, published by TD Economics on Wednesday prior to the Canada-EU summit taking place in Montreal on Thursday and Friday, said current Canadian access to European markets is limited due to regulatory hurdles, geography and other factors.

“These barriers notwithstanding, Canada is well positioned to increase its market share in the EU,” wrote report authors and TD economists Vikram Rai and Rishi Sondhi.

They said this week’s summit is an opportunity to “build momentum and advance cooperation in priority sectors,” as Canada looks to diversify its trading partnerships amid an ongoing trade war with the U.S.

“European demand increasingly overlaps with Canadian capabilities and the two sides’ strategic interest in diversifying economic ties,” the report said.

“The upside for Canadian exports is meaningful. Product-level analysis suggests demand for nearly $60 billion in additional goods exports could exist, under certain conditions, including roughly $50 billion in energy.”

The report listed the defence, energy, critical minerals, digital markets, and financial and other professional services sectors as those with the “largest long-term opportunities” in an expanded Canada-EU trade partnership.

“The biggest gains will need to be unlocked through expanded infrastructure and deeper cooperation to expand investment, improve market access, and build new supply chains in critical areas,” it said.

Trade currently limited

The EU accounts for around five per cent of Canada’s total international goods exports, the report noted, roughly in line with Canadian exports to the U.K. and China. Last year, it amounted to $43 billion worth of merchandise, which was just one per cent of the EU’s total imports.

“Canada’s main exports to the EU include crude oil, aircraft, aluminum, uranium, iron, canola, nickel and diamonds,” the report said.

“Even with this hefty product mix, Canada typically runs a goods trade deficit with the EU. In 2025, it amounted to $50 billion, with Canada importing high-value manufactured products like pharmaceutical products, automobiles and medical instruments.”

Trade, the report argues, is the “most obvious place” for Canada and the EU to deepen their economic partnership, and the report authors said there are two main ways to think about the opportunity.

“The first is to look for products Canada already exports competitively but sells only in small amounts to Europe,” they said.

“The second is to focus on strategic sectors – such as energy and critical minerals – where governments on both sides want to build new supply chains and deepen economic ties, even if trade is limited today.”

Breaking down economic and trade barriers for goods and services is something both Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have advocated for as Canada and the EU discuss what a closer relationship will ultimately look like.

This week’s summit may provide some answers, but there’s still a long way to go, the report authors say.

“Much work will remain after the summit: securing capital and buyers, delivering timely approvals, expanding infrastructure, and easing certification and procurement barriers,” they said.

“Ultimately, stronger demand, greater Canadian capacity and better market access – not a one-off diversion of trade – could make Europe a meaningfully larger export market.”

items.body:
Darren Sissons, Partner & Portfolio Manager, Campbell, Lee & Ross Investment Management

Focus: Global & Technology Stocks

Top Picks: Atlas Copco AB, Brookfield Corp, Crombie REIT

Looking forward, two thorny catalysts are quietly unfolding that will drive both positive and negative market impacts.

The first is the U.S. midterm elections. Current polling suggests the U.S. President will become a lame duck during his remaining two years in office. Given his unconventional style, expect more executive orders and heightened volatility.

The second is building inflationary pressure. The Bank of Canada raised interest rates by 0.25 on October 28, 2026, with further increases likely. Equally concerning is the 79 per cent probability of a 0.25 per cent increase in U.S. interest rates following the December U.S. Federal Reserve meeting.

Rising Canadian interest rates will positively impact the Canadian dollar, reducing imported inflation and making foreign travel cheaper. Unfortunately, higher rates increase debt-servicing costs, reducing demand for new loans from corporates and consumers. Collectively, rising rates will slow the economy at a critical time when U.S. tariffs are already biting.

The counterbalance is the discounted entry levels available in rate-sensitive sectors, i.e., pipelines, real estate investment trusts (REITs), telecommunications, and utilities. Elevated yields combined with attractive entry levels, particularly among companies with intact growth catalysts, are a positive. Additionally, heightened volatility will provide opportunities to add inexpensive exposure to quality names and enable profit-taking on overbought securities.

A brief word of caution on tax-loss selling. Given the strong markets under Trump 2.0, risk-managed portfolio trimming and repositioning throughout 2026 generated sizable tax liabilities. Be mindful of companies currently being sold for tax-loss purposes, as the transition into the new tax year may see investor sentiment reverse from selling to buying.

  • Sign up for the Market Call Top Picks newsletter at bnnbloomberg.ca/newsletters

Atlas Copco AB (ATCO B SS)

A progressive dividend currently yielding 1.85 per cent. It is the leading global vacuum franchise, with exposure to four segments: compressor technique (47 per cent of revenue), vacuum technique (23 per cent), industrial technique (17 per cent), and power technique (13 per cent).

Vacuum technology is a major beneficiary of semiconductor production, as the clean rooms use vacuum technology during semiconductor fabrication.

It operates an asset-light business model, focusing primarily on value-added activities such as design, procurement, research and development, and marketing, while outsourcing lower-value-added functions.

The company’s tuck-in acquisition program acquires numerous companies annually, both to enter new markets and geographies and to expand product offerings.

We are long-term owners, which has generated a multiple on our cost base.

It sold off somewhat in 2026 so is attractively priced, despite generating a 10-year annualized total return in Canadian dollars of 17 per cent per annum.

Brookfield Corp (BN TSX)

An irregular dividend currently yielding 0.73 per cent. It is a leading global private capital franchise with exposure to real estate, infrastructure, private equity, and liquid strategies.

Corporate cash flows are best understood through the lens of distributable earnings (DE), which encompass operating results, gains on divestitures, and profit-sharing on invested funds. DE, which has typically grown at a low-teens annual rate, is a key driver of total assets and shareholder equity growth, which compounded at annual averages growth rates of 16 per cent and 15 per cent, respectively, over the past 15 years.

Brookfield is attractively priced. Like its peers, concerns over private debt exposure, have weighed on its shares driving a 19 per cent discount vis-à-vis 12 months ago. The discounting has created an attractive entry point for new investors.

Despite the 2026 sell-off, the company has still generated an annualized total return of 13.4 per cent since 2016.

Crombie REIT (CRR.UN TSX)

A sustainable dividend currently yielding 5.70 per cent. The lion’s share of the rent roll is supported by essential and investment-grade tenants, including Empire Company Limited banners (Sobeys, Safeway, FreshCo, and Farm Boy), which account for approximately half of annual rental income. The majority of the remaining rent residual is generated by Shoppers Drug Mart, Dollarama, Canadian chartered banks (CIBC, BMO, and Scotiabank), and federal and provincial government offices.

Crombie trades at an attractive entry level as, like its interest-rate-sensitive peers, its units have declined to a 15 per cent discount to Net Asset Value (NAV) due to concerns over rising interest rates.

For income investors, the sustainable yield and valuation discount provide optionality through both earnings’ growth and potential capital appreciation as the discount to NAV discount narrows.

items.title: Canada quietly abandoned promise to end thermal coal exports, audit says
items.description: Environment and Climate Change Canada abandoned its work on ending thermal coal exports without ever notifying the public and without any record of being directed to do so, according to a new audit.

items._ogDesc: Environment and Climate Change Canada abandoned its work on ending thermal coal exports without ever notifying the public and without any record of being directed to do so, according to a new audit.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- Environment and Climate Change Canada abandoned its work on ending thermal coal exports without ever notifying the public and without any record of being directed to do so, according to a new audit.

A report from the office of the auditor general, tabled Thursday, criticized the move and pointed out that Canada is co-chair of an international alliance meant to help countries transition away from coal.

Burning coal is one of the most polluting forms of electricity generation. In 2021, Canada committed to banning thermal coal exports by 2030.

The audit found that while Environment Canada worked for three years to find a way to enforce the ban, that work stopped altogether in November 2024 after lobbying from the coal industry.

“The department did not produce evidence of an official direction to discontinue work on the ban in 2024,” the audit said.

Even the work to enforce the ban was scaled down before Ottawa ultimately gave up on it.

The audit found that between October 2021 and February 2024, Environment Canada officials were trying to use existing laws to enforce the export ban -- including by regulating it as a toxic substance, similarly to what Ottawa is doing now with single-use plastics.

The audit said that by February 2024, those efforts shifted to considering non-regulatory approaches, including “voluntary measures,” though it doesn’t say exactly what those measures were.

The decision to stop the work wasn’t formalized until August 2025, when the federal government was looking for cost-saving measures, said the audit. Still, Ottawa didn’t tell the public.

“However, we also found no clear records to show that the department had provided the minister with an assessment of the implications of stopping all work on the export ban,” the audit report said.

“While the commitment had been announced internationally and noted in multiple federal strategies, the work on the ban was stopped with no public announcement.”

Thermal coal exports were higher in 2025 than they were in 2021, the audit report says.

The report criticized the government’s secrecy on the file.

“The lack of public information and updates on the government’s current approach is concerning,” it said.

“Transparency in decision making provides certainty and enables interested parties, such as provincial and territorial governments, coal mining companies, transportation authorities, shipping terminals, and the labour force to contribute to a just transition.”

The report said 61 per cent of thermal coal shipped from Canadian ports in 2025 came up from the United States, largely from Washington, Oregon and California.

The American mines send it by train north to shipping terminals in British Columbia, mainly because regulations in the U.S. make it challenging to build export infrastructure along the Pacific coast to ship to Asian markets.

Former B.C. premier David Eby suggested that Ottawa could use Canada’s role in facilitating exports of U.S. thermal coal as leverage in trade negotiations.

In August, Eby -- apparently unaware Ottawa already had abandoned the work -- told reporters the federal government should move faster to phase out exports of thermal coal.

Thursday’s reports from the auditor general’s office also looked into Global Affairs Canada’s role in overseeing $16 billion in commitments to international coal transition programs.

Canada committed $15 billion to the Women-Led Coal Transition Mechanism, and another $1 billion in low-interest loans to the Climate Investment Funds’ Accelerating Coal Transition investment program, which is jointly funded by Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany and Denmark. That $1-billion investment made up 42 per cent of the program’s funding, the audit found.

“For Global Affairs Canada, this contribution was also one of the department’s single largest project investments ever made,” the report said.

“The program finances country‑led investment plans with projects designed to accelerate coal retirement, scale up clean energy alternatives, and mitigate socio‑economic impacts on affected workers and communities. Projects are expected to continue up to 2047.”

The audit reported Environment Canada never informed Global Affairs Canada of the decision to stop work in November 2024.

“We found that Global Affairs Canada was involved in the work on the thermal coal export ban only at the request of Environment and Climate Change Canada,” the report said.

“In accordance with its responsibilities for foreign affairs and trade policy, Global Affairs Canada provided information on the trade risks associated with potential implementation options for a thermal coal export ban.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

items.title: Ottawa launches telecom road map to improve competition, consumer choice
items.description: The federal government says it is launching a road map to boost competition and choice within Canada’s telecommunications sector.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A cell tower is pictured in rural Ontario on Wednesday, July 15, 2020. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Sean Kilpatrick]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The federal government says it is launching a road map to boost competition and choice within Canada’s telecommunications sector.
items.body:
The federal government says it is launching a road map to boost competition and choice within Canada’s telecommunications sector.

The plan, announced late Wednesday by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, is meant to break down regional barriers and promote cross-Canada competition in the internet and mobile services sector. It incorporates many policies already unveiled by the federal government and CRTC in recent years, while also outlining a strategy for future actions.

In the road map, the government said it is helping to give consumers more choices and make it easier for providers to access existing networks, or expand the infrastructure they own.

“As the global economy rapidly evolves, Canadians are increasingly relying on telecommunications services in their everyday lives,” said Joly in a statement.

“By improving competition, empowering consumers and supporting the expansion of networks and services, this road map truly puts Canadians first, through actions that will improve choice, transparency, prices and networks.”

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The strategy highlights previously introduced regulations, such as those requiring large internet providers to open up their networks to competitors who can resell service to customers in exchange for a fee.

While the rules were initially touted as a way to help smaller companies compete, they also allow large companies to resell internet using their rivals’ networks outside their core regions. Both Telus Corp. and Bell Canada have begun offering fibre service to customers in each other’s dominant territory under the framework.

The policy applies only to existing fibre networks, and any new fibre built by the large telecoms can’t be made available to competitors until 2029.

The government also wants to help consumers take advantage of more affordable plans, noting cellular plan prices are down 49 per cent compared with 2019. It said the government “will spotlight” competitive offers on the market, make it easier to shop around and switch providers, and eliminate unnecessary fees.

Much of that work has been prioritized over the past year by the telecommunications regulator.

In June, the CRTC banned companies from charging fees to activate, change or cancel a plan — a move the government estimates will save consumers $100 million per year — and other new rules require providers to offer self‑serve options to switch or end plans and provide end-of-contract notifications.

Beginning next March, a new policy will also take effect requiring internet providers to disclose certain information via a standardized label when promoting their plans. They must advertise typical speeds associated with a plan during hours of peak usage and list the monthly price after any promotion ends.

Part of the road map appears to respond to industry concerns in recent years, with major players frequently highlighting the need to ensure regulatory policies create incentives for them to invest in new technologies and infrastructure.

The government said it will help companies deploy the latest fibre-optic networks, experiment with new technologies and strengthen access to connectivity in northern, rural and Indigenous communities.

It plans to release more 5G spectrum — the electromagnetic frequencies that enable smartphone communications — over the next three years, which will increase the total spectrum available for wireless services five-fold. Canadians can also expect increased satellite-based cellular and internet services as the technology continues to evolve, the document said.

Last week, a new report from U.K.-based Global System for Mobile Communications Association said the focus of Canada’s telecom policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions for companies to invest in their networks, citing that traditional revenues are plateauing and capital costs are expected to rise. The paper called for a “policy reset” that prioritizes affordable and predictable spectrum pricing, support for 5G and AI infrastructure such as data centres, and improved regulatory certainty.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has previously hinted at an eagerness to help the industry’s infrastructure needs. Last month, while speaking at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, Carney said the government planned to help “finance new nation-building infrastructure, including a sovereign broadband backbone that connects Canadians from coast to coast to coast with more direct and secure links to Europe and Asia.”

Last year’s federal budget also announced a new “dig once” policy approach, which is meant to encourage telecom companies to co-ordinate when installing fibre optic lines as part of the development of major projects such as energy transmission, railways, pipelines, and roads and highways.

The road map released this week said that strategy could result in significant savings for companies, with studies having shown that 75 to 90 per cent of the cost of a fibre project comes from construction and labour activity rather than the fibre itself.

Meanwhile, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada is consulting on changes to speed up wireless tower approvals, the road map noted.

It said the CRTC will also speed up how it handles disputes between providers, using tools such as mediation and administrative penalties to ensure companies meet their obligations.

The Canadian Telecommunications Association said Ottawa’s priority should be building on progress that has already seen prices come down for consumers “by ensuring that Canada’s telecommunications policies support both competition and the substantial private investment needed.”

“Measures that make it easier to invest and deploy advanced networks, including making more spectrum available for wireless services, implementing ‘dig once’ policies, streamlining wireless tower approvals, and reducing red tape and unnecessary regulatory burdens, are particularly important,” said spokesperson Nick Kyonka in a statement.

“Policies that balance competition with the need for sustainable investment are essential to delivering lasting benefits for consumers and supporting Canada’s broader economic ambitions.”

The government plans to monitor progress of its various goals through indicators such as prices, switching behaviour, network speeds, coverage and consumer complaints.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

Canada’s much-anticipated summit with the European Union begins today after months of speculation around how a new alliance between the two bodies will take shape.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made headlines last month when she publicly invited Prime Minister Mark Carney to grow the Canada-EU relationship, floating the term “associate member” in a speech. Some countries have pushed back on that label, and Canadian officials have called the partnership an “alliance for the future.”

Carney has pushed for closer ties with global partners while Ottawa and Washington spar in a trade war that has dragged on throughout U.S. President Donald Trump’s term.

items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.

He made the announcement today as he welcomed European Union leaders to Montreal for a summit aimed at forging closer ties.

In April, Cohere announced it would merge with Germany’s Aleph Alpha and said the company would be “anchored in” Germany and Canada.

Carney said that, under the agreement, Cohere will stay Canadian.

He said the company will invest at least $1.7 billion in new computing infrastructure in Canada and partner on research with Canadian institutions.

Carney said Canada won’t wait for the future of artificial intelligence to be decided elsewhere by those we don’t know or trust.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

items.body:
Toymaker Spin Master Corp. said it’s keeping prices steady heading into the holiday shopping season despite tariffs and rising manufacturing costs.

Chief executive Christina Miller said the company has maintained its pricing strategy, with roughly half of its products priced below US$20.

“We continue to have about 50 per cent of our products priced below the $19.99 range,” she said during an earnings call on Thursday.

  • Latest updates on company news here

Miller said the toymaker’s prices help make its products affordable to families across different income levels.

Spin Master reported a third-quarter profit of US$79 million, down from US$106.8 million in the same quarter last year.

The company said strong demand for the Paw Patrol and Melissa & Doug brands helped offset weakness elsewhere in its business.

The company’s latest movie, “Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie” released in August, helped drive the toymaker’s entertainment revenue, which jumped 61 per cent to US$52.8 million from US$32.8 million a year earlier. 

Spin Master CFO Jonathan Roiter said the company expects demand for dinosaur-themed toys and merchandise tied to the latest movie to continue well into 2027.

“We think there’s long legs with the dino theme,” he said, referring to the staying power of dinosaur-inspired rescue vehicles, figures and playsets. 

Roiter said the company’s upcoming fourth-quarter results remain highly dependent on consumer demand and retailer replenishment orders.

He said about half of its annual retail toy sales occur in the fourth quarter.

Looking ahead to 2027, Spin Master said its growth drivers include Melissa & Doug, Monster Jam, GUND, Stickerbox and a new trading-card game.

  • Latest updates on investing here

The company said Melissa & Doug sales increased approximately 10 per cent during the quarter, supported by more shelf space, international expansion and new products.

The toymaker, which keeps its books in U.S. dollars, said its profit amounted to 77 cents US per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30, down from US$1.03 per diluted share a year earlier.

On an adjusted basis, Spin Master said it earned US$1.03 per diluted share in its latest quarter, down from US$1.11 per diluted share in the same quarter last year.

Revenue for the quarter totalled US$732.7 million, down from US$734.7 million a year ago.

The company also announced it has named Kate Rouch to its board of directors. 

Rouch is a former OpenAI executive where she was its first chief marketing officer and has also held leadership positions at Meta and Coinbase.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Canada has launched an updated framework for national security with a call to prepare for all emergencies, including the possibility of war.
items.body:
Canada has launched an updated framework for national security with a call to prepare for all emergencies, including the possibility of war.

The release of the plan comes as the trade war with the United States deepens. Since becoming president, Donald Trump has continued to threaten turning Canada into the 51st state.

In a recent interview with the New York Times, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he studied the “extreme tail risk” of a U.S. military action against Canada.

During a background briefing with reporters, a senior government official said the plan is about “preparing for all contingencies in worst-case scenarios up to war.”

“We do think it is high time that all of Canada, Canadian businesses, and Canadian academics are more aware of the external threat environment and that we as a country are more prepared for the threats that Canada faces.”

Protecting Canada’s eight strategic economic sectors is a key focus of the strategy. Those sectors include emerging technologies, critical minerals, defence, energy, transportation, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology, food security and financial transactions.

The previous national security framework, drafted more than 20 years ago, did not lay out a plan to protect the economy.

The United States is the only country explicitly named in the framework, although regions such as Europe, the Middle East and the Indo-Pacific are referenced.

The first line of the policy states: “True Sovereignty allows Canadians to live our lives as we choose.”

During a background briefing, a panel of security officials said the strategy will involve new legislation based on five pillars: security, foreign relations, defence, public safety and intelligence.

The first changes will be introduced next month in a new foreign policy that lists building a new partnership with the United States as a priority.

items.title: Equitable Bank to sell Bennington Financial to Desjardins Group
items.description: EQB offloads its equipment leasing arm to Desjardins as it sharpens focus on core growth
items.content: <p>EQB offloads its equipment leasing arm to Desjardins as it sharpens focus on core growth</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288916419378197.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: EQB offloads its equipment leasing arm to Desjardins as it sharpens focus on core growth
items.body:
Equitable Bank, the Toronto-based lender that routes its alternative mortgages exclusively through Canada’s broker channel, has agreed to sell its commercial equipment leasing subsidiary, Bennington Financial Corp., to Desjardins Group.

The deal marks another step in EQB Inc.’s deliberate exit from non-core businesses. It follows their acquisition of PC Financial, which closed in July and added nearly four million customers.

Desjardins Group will acquire 100% of Bennington’s shares at a price equivalent to an approximately 8% discount to lease receivables.

As at July 31, Bennington’s aggregate portfolio held roughly $1.1 billion in lease receivables. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027. 

EQB will reclassify Bennington as held for sale and record a net after-tax charge in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, treated as an adjusting item.

The deal is expected to be relatively neutral to Equitable Bank’s common equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio at closing.

Chadwick Westlake, President and Chief Executive Officer of EQB Inc. in Toronto, Ontario, said the divestiture is a natural extension of the bank’s recalibrated priorities.

“At EQB, we’re focused on doing more of what we do best and investing where we see the greatest opportunity to win,” he said.

“This transaction allows us to further concentrate our capital and resources on our core growth priorities, particularly following our PC Financial transaction. It also positions Bennington with an owner that is equipped to grow the business to its full potential with expertise in the sector. Consistent with other businesses and product exits over the past year, this move strengthens our ability to create value for customers and shareholders over the long term.”

A pattern of deliberate portfolio exits

The Bennington sale continues a visible pivot at EQB. Since completing the acquisition of PC Financial, EQB has moved steadily to shed businesses that no longer align with its core focus.

Canadian Mortgage Professional has followed EQB’s most profitable year on record, when annual revenue surpassed $1 billion for the first time in fiscal 2025.

The broker channel remains central to that model; as one Equitable Bank executive previously confirmed to Canadian Mortgage Professional, “We continue to believe that the best way in this country to get a mortgage is through a mortgage broker.”

A strategic fit for Desjardins

Denis Dubois, President and CEO of Desjardins Group in Lévis, Québec, said the deal complements the cooperative’s existing business financing capabilities.

“Bennington’s specialized expertise in commercial equipment leasing and financing makes it a strong strategic fit for Desjardins,” he said.

“This transaction brings capabilities that complement our existing business financing offering and support our growth ambitions across Canada, while providing a strong foundation for Bennington to continue building on its established business, expertise and relationships.”

Desjardins Group is a financial cooperative, offering personal and business banking, wealth management, and insurance services to more than 10 million members and clients, with total net revenue of $16.31 billion and total assets of $510.2 billion in fiscal 2025.

National Bank Capital Markets and McCarthy Tétrault LLP are advising EQB on the transaction. Desjardins Capital Markets and Norton Rose Fulbright Canada LLP are advising Desjardins.

items.title: Prime rate hits 4.70% today as big banks act on BoC hike
items.description: Variable-rate mortgage and HELOC borrowers face higher costs today as Canada’s big six banks move
items.content: <p>Variable-rate mortgage and HELOC borrowers face higher costs today as Canada’s big six banks move</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288897773939059.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Variable-rate mortgage and HELOC borrowers face higher costs today as Canada’s big six banks move
items.body:
Canada’s variable-rate mortgage holders and home equity line of credit (HELOC) borrowers are paying more as of today, after the country’s six largest banks put a new prime lending rate of 4.70% into effect. 

The move follows the Bank of Canada’s (BoC) decision to raise its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on Wednesday, its first increase since 2023.

The Royal Bank of Canada (RBC), Toronto-Dominion Bank (TD), Bank of Montreal (BMO), Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC), Bank of Nova Scotia (Scotiabank), and National Bank of Canada each implemented the quarter-point increase, moving in lockstep from a prime rate of 4.45% that had been in place since October 2025.

TD also raised its separate mortgage prime rate — the benchmark used to price its variable-rate mortgage products — to 4.85% from 4.60%, a spread that sits 15 basis points above its standard prime.

For borrowers on fixed-payment variable mortgages, today’s change means a larger share of each instalment goes toward interest rather than principal. Those on adjustable-payment structures will see monthly costs rise immediately.

A housing market that wasn’t moving before today

The effective rate increase reaches a market that had already gone quiet.

Phil Soper, president and chief executive of Royal LePage in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional this month that anticipated buyer pull-ahead had not materialised even as rate-hike speculation intensified.

“You’d see some people that were planning to get into the market in the spring of 2027, for example, jumping in now to get ahead of anticipated higher borrowing costs. Yet we’re not seeing material changes in the trajectory of transaction volumes. It’s very flat,” Soper said.

Benjamin Reitzes of BMO says the Bank of Canada's first rate hike in more than three years may not be its last, with future decisions likely hinging on economic growth, inflation trends, and incoming data over the months ahead. https://t.co/lcW0HncB9d — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 29, 2026

What brokers need to tell clients today

Leah Zlatkin, mortgage broker and expert at LowestRates.ca, said in April that borrower psychology still carries heavy residue from the previous hiking cycle.

“Most borrowers still prefer the certainty of fixed payments, especially after the sharp increases to variable rates during the Bank of Canada’s rate-hiking cycle in 2022 and 2023,” Zlatkin said. That hesitancy only deepens with today’s move confirmed.

“Variable rates come with uncertainty,” she added. “Borrowers need to be comfortable with the possibility that rates could move higher again depending on how the economic environment evolves.”

Victor Tran, spokesperson at Rates.ca, shared earlier this year that despite growing curiosity around variable products, fixed-rate mortgages still dominate client decisions.

“Most households are still opting for fixed because it offers predictability in an environment where rate direction isn’t guaranteed,” Tran said.

items.description: What higher borrowing costs could mean for homebuying and the renewal wave
items.content: <p>What higher borrowing costs could mean for homebuying and the renewal wave</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639288862172865356.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: What higher borrowing costs could mean for homebuying and the renewal wave
items.body:
Fixed mortgage rates have been on the rise amid climbing bond yields in recent weeks and the Bank of Canada is now back in hiking mode, putting upward pressure on variable rates.

National homebuying activity was already weak before the central bank’s 25-basis-point hike on Wednesday, but mortgage industry figures fear the move could worsen the outlook for the housing market even further.

The Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA-ON) said it was “disappointed” by the BoC’s move, describing it as a decision that could have a big negative impact on consumer and investor confidence in a market that’s already been weighed down by global economic uncertainty and trade tensions.

Jessica Rickerby, CMBA-ON president, suggested that the decision had prioritized inflation over housing challenges. “While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability,” she said in remarks accompanying the statement.

“The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is – at present – only slightly above the Bank of Canada’s target rate.”

Higher rates have implications for the renewal picture

The recent jump in fixed rates has seen a growing number of Canadians turn away from those options and toward sometimes shorter-term variable options, a trend noted by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) in its latest residential mortgage industry report.

The much-discussed mortgage renewal wave, in which scores of pandemic-era mortgages have renewed at higher interest rates in 2025 and 2026, seemed to be past its peak. But if rates continue rising – and Canadians are increasingly choosing shorter mortgage terms – that could prolong renewal challenges, according to CMHC’s deputy chief economist Aled ab Iorwerth (pictured top).

“There is a move away from the five-year fixed towards shorter-term mortgages,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “And interest rates have been going up. So I’m a little bit more concerned than I used to be in that area.

“I’m a little bit concerned that we’re going to have more of this discussion of renewal at higher interest rates. Perhaps my concerns won’t materialize – and I hope they don’t – but that is certainly an area that I’m more concerned about than I used to be.”

That’s not to say a series of big rate hikes by the Bank of Canada is in store. Instead, ab Iorwerth’s main concern is wider pressure in the lending system with the potential to drive bond yields and interest rates higher.

“US fiscal deficits, demand for money for AI, saving from an aging population – I see a lot of demand for savings, putting upward pressure on, say, five-year interest rates,” he said. “I wouldn’t tie it directly to the Bank of Canada. There’s going to be a lot of demand for money in order to invest in a range of different options.”

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, the BoC’s senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers indicated the central bank wasn’t expecting the housing market to pick up pace any time soon.

“Certainly, borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market,” Rogers said after the Bank’s announcement. “An increase will add to that a bit on the margin, so I think the outlook we’ve got for housing in the forecast… takes all of that into account.”

What the hike means for commercial mortgages

Rising bond yields and inflation concerns have clouded the outlook for the commercial lending sector – but Mark Fieder, principal and president at Avison Young Canada, struck a bullish tone on the space’s prospects after the BoC’s latest move.

“Despite this rate hike, we anticipate demand for institutional-quality commercial real estate will remain strong,” he said, “supported by durable income, downside protection, and long-term portfolio stability.

“Pricing for premier assets will stay competitive, particularly in the industrial and multifamily sectors. Transaction activity will be increasingly governed by asset quality, lease profile, and growth prospects.”

items._ogDesc: Ontario’s deficit has grown by more than $3 billion in the past few months as the province continues to face economic headwinds blowing up from the U.S.
items.body:
Ontario’s deficit has grown by more than $3 billion in the past few months as the province continues to face economic headwinds blowing up from the U.S.

In an economic update delivered on Thursday, the Ford government said the deficit for 2026-27 is now projected to be $16.9 billion, up from the $13.8 billion that was projected in the budget tabled back in March.

“Our government continues to face significant economic uncertainty driven by U.S. tariffs on Canada, but our government has a plan to protect workers, businesses and communities while building a stronger economy for the future,” Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy said in a written statement accompanying his fall economic statement.

Most of the measures to do so have previously been announced. They include the joint $8.7 billion Canada-Ontario action plan with the federal government to bolster the steel, automotive and critical mineral sectors, as well as a recently announced plan to provide $8 billion in provincial tax relief to businesses by allowing them to write off a wide arrange of assets, another joint venture with the feds.

Some of the higher deficit owes to boosted funding to the government’s contingency and reserve funds.

Ontario has increased funding in its fiscal reserve fund from $1.5 billion to $2.2 billion. The province says the increase reflects “ongoing extraordinary circumstances, including significant trade-related risks to Ontario’s economic outlook.”

Smaller deficits of $12.7 billion and $6.7 billion are expected over the next two fiscal years, with a small surplus of $200 million projected for 2029-30. The government had projected in the spring budget that it hoped to return to balance in 2028-29 with a surplus of $600 million.

The government says that despite the economic uncertainty, the province’s economy is expected to continue growing. Real GDP is projected to increase by just 0.5 per cent in 2026 and 1.5 per cent in 2027.

Corporate tax up, person income tax down

The higher deficit comes even as overall government revenue is actually up, now projected at $2 billion higher than the $232.6 billion forecast in the spring budget. The government says this is due to higher-than-expected federal transfers, as well as $878 million more in sales tax and around $1.5 billion more in corporate tax revenue.

At the same time, the province has seen revenue drop in other areas. Revenue from personal income tax is $1.7 billion less than previously forecast, due to less-than-expected revenue from the CRA for 2025. Government officials say this mainly reflects less capital gains tax revenue than expected and also stems from difficulties in projecting personal income revenue.

The province is also now projecting $3.28 billion in Land Transfer Tax revenue, $497 million less than forecasted in the budget. That’s mainly owing to the sluggish housing market, the government says.

To help make up the shortfall, the government is borrowing $3.9 billion more, bringing long-term borrowing to $51.1 billion.

While the government is projecting a return to balance in three years, a slower-growth scenario contemplates more large deficits over the next few years, while a faster-growth scenario could see the province return to balance as soon as 2028-29.

Unemployment in the province sits at 7.2 per cent for 2026, but the government says it expects that to decrease to 6.1 per cent in 2029 with strengthening economic growth.

Other highlights

  • The province says it is increasing the penalty for people who fraudulently claim the first-time homebuyers’ credit
  • Ontario is capping the monthly credit for the Ontario Electricity Rebate at 1,200 KWh for residential customers as of May 1, 2027. The government says this will maintain affordability and ensure stability. The average residential customer uses 700KWh.
  • The $4 billion Protect Ontario Investment Fund announced in the spring budget has now been paused as the government explores possible better uses for the funds in the wake of further instability
  • The province is proposing narrowing the Ontario Computer Animation and Special Effects Tax Credit so that just TV and film producers will be eligible, a move asked for by the industry to help support it.

items.title: The big question: How many more BoC rate hikes are ahead?
items.description: The central bank delivered a 25-basis-point increase on Wednesday, and it may not be done yet
items.content: <p>The central bank delivered a 25-basis-point increase on Wednesday, and it may not be done yet</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639288097708752714.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The central bank delivered a 25-basis-point increase on Wednesday, and it may not be done yet
items.body:
The Bank of Canada delivered its first interest rate hike for over three years on Wednesday, sparking immediate questions about how far – and how fast – it might raise rates if it decides further increases are needed.

The central bank’s decision moved its benchmark rate to 2.5%, and its accompanying statement was frank that more hikes could be ahead if the inflation outlook worsens again.

For now, much will depend on the economic and inflation data that emerges in the months ahead, Bank of Montreal (BMO) managing director, Canadian rates and macro strategist Benjamin Reitzes told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

“It’s a little bit early to say how far they’ll go,” Reitzes said. “Looking at market pricing, there’s [a benchmark rate of] about 3.5% by the end of next year, a little further out. And that’s a bit on the aggressive side, I think.

“Getting that high suggests that you’d need a trade deal and some pretty good economic outcomes for that to come to fruition.”

At least one more hike seemingly ahead

It’s still safe to assume that the central bank will raise rates at least once more in the next several months, Reitzes said, either in December or January. The extent of the economy’s weakness in the coming weeks will be a crucial deciding factor in the timing of the next hike.

“The reason for their caution is that they have a pretty soft [GDP] forecast for the fourth quarter, just 0.8% growth,” he said. “If you have that amount of softness in the economy, do they really want to be hiking rates in that environment? The answer is probably no.

“They want to make sure that there is a rebound in growth. So if we do get some numbers coming over the next few weeks that point to a better fourth quarter, then that would be enough for them to likely [hike]. But we don’t get a lot of pieces of information between now and December, unfortunately.”

Central bank governor Tiff Macklem highlighted that persistent lack of clarity in remarks at the press conference following the announcement – a situation that’s exacerbated by ongoing geopolitical chaos.

“We are mindful that uncertainty is still elevated,” he said. “Developments in the Middle East and Canada-US trade relations both remain fluid.”

Inflation concerns persist amid rising fuel costs

The annual inflation rate ticked higher in September, increasing to 3.1% amid continuing upward pressure on fuel prices caused by the US-Iran war.

Some economists viewed that as a mild enough reading for the BoC to keep rates steady in today’s announcement, but a growing number indicated a pre-emptive increase by the central bank was the likeliest outcome of its October decision.

Macklem said fuel costs would probably start to impact other types of inflation if they remain elevated. “The longer energy prices remain high, the more likely it is these costs will spill over to consumer prices more broadly,” he said.

But the consumer price index (CPI) is still well below its 2022 level, when it ballooned to a 39-year high and prompted a flurry of big BoC rate hikes. The current environment, Reitzes said, is a “different world” to that era – mainly because of the weak growth outlook.

That means a steady stream of rate hikes by the central bank in the coming months remains unlikely for now.

“The likelihood of that resuming or something like that seems pretty low. We don’t have the level of stimulus globally that we had in the economy at that time,” he said. “You don’t have governments around the world pouring money into the economy and the post-pandemic surge in demand.

“We don’t have that type of event coming at this point. It’s more energy-price-driven. And we’ll see how the war in the Middle East goes. It’s just not the same backdrop – and the Bank just wants to make sure that they don’t let inflation take root again and have to deal with broader price pressures and then have to raise rates more aggressively later.”

items.title: BoC warns of 'subdued' outlook for housing market as rate hike raises borrowing costs
items.description: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.

The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent, the first increase in more than three years, as it warned that inflation driven by the war in the Middle East is likely to spread.

"There's a number of things weighing on housing right now," the bank's senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers told reporters, as she described a "subdued" outlook for the sector.

"Certainly, borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market. An increase will add to that a bit on the margin, so I think the outlook we've got for housing in the forecast here takes all of that into account."

The big question is whether the central bank's move is a one-time adjustment or the start of a sustained tightening cycle, said Phil Soper, president and CEO of real estate firm Royal LePage.

He said the sector's "prolonged weakness is already weighing on economic growth, and higher borrowing costs will only deepen that challenge."

Shawn Zigelstein, a broker for Royal LePage Signature Realty, said he believes the rate hike won't have a major effect on consumer confidence just yet.

"It's not like we are in a market like we were back in 2022 where the prices are increasing substantially on a regular basis," he said in an interview.

"A quarter-point adjustment really shouldn't make too much of a difference on someone's mortgage payments at this point."

The central bank's key policy rate had held steady for nearly a year following a series of cuts. Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent in September due to high gas prices, and the bank said an increase to the rate is necessary to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill over to other goods and services.

Zigelstein said clients he speaks with are more concerned about other day-to-day costs and whether the overall inflation environment makes it the right time to buy a home.

"They have been worried about other factors, including tariffs and such. Are they going to have the jobs that they had? Are their investments going to do what they've been doing? So they've got bigger concerns than worrying about interest rates," he said.

"Now, of course, if the rates start to change a little bit, then we will start to see potentially a little bit of a pullback on what people are spending because borrowing costs will be higher."

While Canada "is not facing a broad mortgage crisis," there are signs of financial pressure concentrated in specific regions such as the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area and southwestern Ontario, said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp., earlier this week.

He said trade tensions are weighing on key manufacturing sectors such as the automotive industry in those areas, leading to labour-market uncertainty and softer housing market conditions.

CMHC said Ontario's mortgage arrears rate reached 0.32 per cent in the second quarter, which is still below historical peaks but expected to continue rising through mid-2027. British Columbia and Atlantic Canada are expected to see a more moderate rise in mortgage arrears over the same period.

"The mortgage system is adjusting, but these early warning signs, particularly in parts of Ontario, need to be monitored closely," ab Iorwerth said in a news release.

Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada, said that while an interest-rate increase "may give some buyers pause," more balanced market conditions in many regions are creating opportunities for buyers, including greater choice and room to negotiate.

In September, the national average sale price fell 1.6 per cent year-over-year to $666,538, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association. National home sales were down 7.7 per cent from the same month last year, as the association cited higher fixed mortgage rates and the Bank of Canada's "notably more hawkish tone."

Fixed rates are largely unaffected by the Bank of Canada's decision, having already moved higher in recent months in line with the bond market. But further movement in the bond market into 2027 could prompt mortgage costs to jump, which "would have a dampening impact on home purchases," said Michael Waters, CEO of Minto Group, a real estate developer.

"Higher rates, everything else held equal, will reduce levels of purchaser activity for anything durable of size — cars and houses, certainly," Waters said in an interview.

"The housing sector is very slow right now and so that obviously would be a concern for anyone in that sector."

Meanwhile, the central bank said Wednesday that higher energy and import costs are expected to raise the costs of housing construction and maintenance through higher prices for materials and equipment.

Any increase to the cost of credit will also have an effect on the ability to build new projects, particularly new housing and supporting infrastructure, said Nicole Emmett, vice-president of communications, marketing and member services for the Canadian Construction Association.

"A home isn’t a home without the roads, sewers and watermains that support it, and higher borrowing costs put pressure on the margins of the contractors building them, which are already stretched by global supply chain disruptions and material costs," she said in a statement.

"Many contractors also rely on financing for equipment, materials and day-to-day operations."

Waters said higher interest — construction loans are based on a floating rate — along with rising input costs "will squeeze margins" and potentially lead to fewer large-scale project completions in the coming years.

"Certainly projects are far more challenged today than they would have been six months ago, pre-Iran war," he said.

"The impact would be fewer projects meeting economic feasibility tests and more projects probably sitting idle until market conditions improve, so that could have a negative impact on the creation of new housing supply."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: Canadian household credit defies renewal shock, CIBC finds
items.description: Mortgage arrears keep rising, but CIBC economists see few cracks across the wider household credit picture
items.content: <p>Mortgage arrears keep rising, but CIBC economists see few cracks across the wider household credit picture</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288083080510285.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage arrears keep rising, but CIBC economists see few cracks across the wider household credit picture
items.body:
Canadian borrowers are absorbing the mortgage renewal shock better than most forecasters expected.

Credit scores are improving and early-stage delinquencies are easing, even as more homeowners fall seriously behind on their mortgages.

That is the conclusion of a new report from CIBC Capital Markets economists Benjamin Tal and Katherine Judge, who revisited household credit quality a year into the mortgage payment cliff.

Their verdict came two days before the Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate to 2.5%.

“Simply put, the credit quality position of Canadian households is surprising on the upside,” they wrote.

Mortgage arrears remain the weak spot

The exception is the mortgage book itself. The share of mortgages 90 or more days in arrears keeps climbing and now sits well above its pre-pandemic level, as borrowers renew at higher rates into a softer labour market.

CIBC estimates that payment jumps of more than 40% hit 5% to 6% of all outstanding mortgages in 2026.

Regionally, the strain is uneven, with mortgage arrears in Ontario expected to keep worsening until mid-2027.

“I think [delinquencies] will continue to increase as more homeowners renew their mortgages in the next 12 months, 24 months even. But I think it’s going to be a slow grind,” Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert at Rates.ca, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year.

Still, serious delinquencies on credit cards and lines of credit held by mortgage borrowers have levelled off. Because most households stop paying those debts before missing a mortgage payment, CIBC treats them as an early warning, and that warning has gone quieter.

Derek Serra of Westboro Mortgage Investment Corporation says the Canadian housing market is still feeling the effects of pandemic-era low interest rates, as borrowers face higher renewal costs and affordability challenges. https://t.co/Dcwt1JphsT — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

Proposals, not bankruptcies

Elsewhere, the numbers point to normalization rather than distress.

Household debt is growing at about 4%, near a record low outside the pandemic, and mortgage balances rose roughly 2% year over year in August, the weakest pace in 25 years. Average credit scores sit 1.3% above 2019 levels.

Insolvencies are up 6% over the year but are only now approaching 2019 levels.

Consumer proposals, which typically cost lenders less than bankruptcies, made up 77% of filings in the third quarter, compared with 60% in 2019. Equifax data on Canada’s insolvency hotspots suggests that choice is deliberate.

“A lot of the insolvency rates that we’re seeing an increase in is really tied to homeowners that want to protect their assets but obviously have a mountain of non-mortgage debt, and they’re trying to find a way to formally reduce that through more structured payments so that they can stay afloat,” Kathy Catsiliras, Equifax Canada’s vice-president of analytics and consulting, told CMP.

CIBC expects renewal payment increases to ease notably from February 2027, with mortgage delinquencies likely to trend lower that year, depending on the job market.

Until then, the Bank of Canada’s first rate hike since 2023 adds pressure where households are already stretched, according to Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright.

“For most people, the 25 basis points on its own isn’t a dramatic change by any means. On a $500,000 mortgage, it’s roughly $60 to $70 more a month, depending on the amortization. The problem is that it can really affect households that have already been struggling,” Fox said.

“Plenty of people locked in at very low rates a few years ago, and they’re now renewing into a much bigger payment. This hike doesn’t help.”

His advice for borrowers nearing renewal: “If you’re renewing in the next year, start early. It’s a good idea to talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up. Pick something you can live with instead of hoping and waiting for rates to fall.”

In partnership with Colliers as a Presenting Sponsor, STOREYS announces Top 75 Real Estate Projects, a new annual report and program built to recognize the most meaningful real estate projects across Canada – from landmark new-builds and redevelopments through to masterplans reshaping entire neighbourhoods, encompassing iconic office buildings, niche industrial centres, master-planned communities, and mixed-use assets.

STOREYS, now in its tenth year, is taking a format with more than two decades of history to the private sector. Top 75 Real Estate Projects builds on the Top 100 Infrastructure Projects report from sister publication ReNew Canada, a mainstay of public sector infrastructure coverage. Now, for the first time, that national framework, editorial rigour, and Top Projects format are being applied to the country’s most significant real estate developments.

Powered by SiteMedia and its seven publications, the inaugural Top 75 Real Estate Projects report is set to become an annual fixture on the Canadian real estate and development calendar.

“From the commercial spaces people work in, to the homes they live in, this list covers the real estate that shapes how Canadians live, work, and invest,” said Andrew Hansen, CEO of Site. “It's a recognition of the projects that raised the bar this year, from masterplans and redevelopments to the condos, rentals, and offices people use every day.”

Colliers joins as the Presenting Sponsor, bringing the scale and expertise of a Canadian commercial real estate leader – with presence coast to coast, from Victoria to Halifax – to ground Top 75 Real Estate Projects in the local data and insight that Colliers’ clients rely on every day, alongside access to its national network of developers, investors, and brokers.

“As a firm with deep Canadian roots, Colliers takes great pride in helping build vibrant structures and communities across the country that positively impact how individuals, companies and communities function and thrive. The Top 75 Real Estate Projects program and report celebrate the local developments and industry players that truly make the greatest difference – this is exactly the type of initiative we are proud to support,” said Lex Perry, Vice President, Marketing, Communications & Research at Colliers in Canada.

Submissions for Top 75 Real Estate Projects open on October 29th, 2026, kicking off a national search for the developments, teams, and ideas setting new standards in Canadian real estate this year.

To submit, visit the website.

The report will launch in September 2027, with launch celebrations slated for Vancouver and Toronto.

With greater than a 30-year track record of consistent growth and strong recurring cash flows, we scale complementary, high-value businesses that provide essential services across the full asset lifecycle. Our unique partnership philosophy empowers exceptional leaders, preserves our entrepreneurial culture, and ensures meaningful inside ownership – driving strong alignment and sustained value creation for our shareholders. items.title: Wealthsimple raises $425M at a $13.8B valuation to fuel growth
items.description: The fintech secures fresh backing as its client base grows to 4 million Canadians
items.content: <p>The fintech secures fresh backing as its client base grows to 4 million Canadians</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/ca/046/0379_637595963905457520.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The fintech secures fresh backing as its client base grows to 4 million Canadians
items.body:
Wealthsimple Technologies Inc. has closed an equity round of up to CAD $425 million at a post-money valuation of CAD $13.8 billion. That's nearly 40% above the CAD $10 billion mark the Toronto-based financial technology company reached in October 2025.

GIC, the Singapore sovereign wealth fund that co-led last year’s fundraise, is again leading the round, alongside Power Corporation of Canada, IGM Financial Inc., ICONIQ, Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) and Inovia.

The deal is structured as a CAD $300 million primary offering alongside a secondary component of up to CAD $125 million, an arrangement designed to let employees share in the value they have helped create.

“This raise reflects the deep conviction our partners have in Wealthsimple’s mission and in our role as the company defining the future of financial services in Canada,” said Michael Katchen, CEO and co-founder of Wealthsimple, in Toronto.

“These investors know our business deeply and chose to increase their commitment. With their support, we will keep building and innovating until every Canadian can live their entire financial life on Wealthsimple.”

Leaving the banks behind

As of September 30, Wealthsimple held CAD $169.2 billion in assets under administration, up 69% from CAD $100 billion at the time of its October 2025 fundraise.

The company now serves more than 4 million Canadians, including one in four aged 18 to 40.

In Q2 2026, new chequing account openings outpaced new investment accounts for the first time in the company’s history.

What it means for mortgage brokers

Wealthsimple’s growing product suite includes a Portfolio Line of Credit, allowing clients to borrow against their investment holdings, alongside a business chequing account, a prepaid Visa card and cash deposit access at more than 5,300 Canada Post locations across Canada.

In the past year, the company launched more than 50 new products spanning trading, chequing and business tools.

As Canadian mortgage industry observers track how fintechs are gaining ground in the mortgage market, the concern is as much about where clients park their savings and equity as it is about which lender wins the deal.

That shift has been closely followed by the sector. Naga Parvatharajan, chief executive of Ratehub.ca in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year – while discussing how OSFI’s new approvals framework is opening the market to fintechs – that greater competition among financial institutions means Canadians gain “better rates and innovative options,” a dynamic that has historically served the broker channel well.

Tanya Woods, head of government and regulatory affairs and policy counsel at Questrade Financial Group, in Toronto, offered broader context to CMP when examining what open banking could mean for Canada’s mortgage market in the years ahead.

" The fact that Canadians might be able to see their entire financial picture on a single dashboard one day is very exciting because they will have a much greater sense of what they can afford and where the opportunities in their financial picture [are], so that they can make different or better decisions on housing," she said.

"Maybe they can afford more than they realized. Maybe they can find new ways to structure their debt because they get a better picture of the types of debt load that they’re carrying and where they can reduce it or leverage it positively. There’s so much opportunity."

items.title: Canada’s rate hike deepens broker worry over a struggling housing market
items.description: Economists call the move preventative; mortgage brokers say affordability remains the real crisis
items.content: <p>Economists call the move preventative; mortgage brokers say affordability remains the real crisis</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288054691670926.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Economists call the move preventative; mortgage brokers say affordability remains the real crisis
items.body:
The Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, 2026, its first increase since 2023, framing the decision as risk management against building inflationary pressure rather than the beginning of a sustained tightening cycle.

Governor Tiff Macklem was direct in his reasoning: “The main argument for an increase was that energy prices are higher, they are expected to remain higher, and cost pressures are building.”

The October Monetary Policy Report (MPR) revised headline inflation to 3.5% by year-end, with the Bank’s 2% target now not expected until mid-2028.

GDP growth projections were upgraded to 1% for 2026 and 2% for 2027, with the Bank’s estimated neutral overnight rate range placed at 2.25% to 3.25%.

Economists divided on the next move

Earlier in the year, Bay Street analysts were actively debating whether a 2026 Bank of Canada rate hike was likely as oil-driven inflation pressure built. That question has now been answered. What remains contested is what follows.

Frances Donald, chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto, and assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen described the decision as “preventative medicine,” noting the Bank’s own MPR acknowledged labour market slack and core inflation near 2%.

“The risks of future inflation were judged to have increased more than downside economic growth risk,” they wrote.

Marc Ercolao, economist at TD Economics in Toronto, characterised the hike as insurance-buying.

“We think this hike buys the Bank a few months to assess whether higher energy and input costs are actually filtering through to consumer prices,” he wrote, forecasting one additional 25-basis-point hike in Q1-2027 that would bring the policy rate to 2.75%, roughly the midpoint of the neutral range.

The central bank said on Wednesday morning it was raising that trendsetting interest rate by 25 basis points to a level of 2.50%, ending its long wait-and-see approach on the rate question. https://t.co/zVa5MRcPZe — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

CIBC economist Andrew Grantham projected a hold in December before a further move in January.

“We don’t expect that core measures of inflation will accelerate as much as the Bank fears, which should become more obvious early in 2027 and allow the Bank of Canada to then hold interest rates at 2.75% throughout the remainder of next year,” he wrote, adding that two-year bond yields barely moved in the wake of the decision.

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres in Vancouver, said the Bank was drawing a direct line to its own recent failures.

“The communications make it clear that the central bank wants to stay ahead of the curve and ‘avoid the debacle’ of 2022-23, when it was too late to raise the policy rate,” she wrote.

Bruno Valko, vice-president of national sales at RMG Mortgage Corporation in Toronto, questioned the Bank’s 2027 inflation projection of 3%, given that WTI crude had surged from approximately $67 per barrel in late February to over $100 per barrel following the US-Iran conflict.

With year-over-year comparisons in 2027 measured against an already elevated 2026 base, Valko argued the maths did not hold.

“Come 2027, when comparing oil prices to 2026, assuming oil continues to hover around $100 per barrel, I dispute the rationale around how inflation can average 3% when it’s currently 3.1%,” he wrote.

Brokers warn of market consequences

For the broker community managing Canada’s mounting 2026 mortgage renewal pressures, the hike arrives at a precarious moment.

Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright, a Toronto-based digital real estate law platform, warned the decision deepens an already prolonged housing downturn.

“A rate hike likely locks us into year-over-year declines in housing activity for the rest of this year and into next, and I don’t see things turning until there’s a rate drop,” Fox said.

His advice to clients approaching renewal was clear, and with the December decision drawing closer, what the BoC’s next decision means for the mortgage market will be watched closely by brokers across the country.

“If you’re renewing in the next year, start early. It’s a good idea to talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up,” Fox said.

The Canadian Mortgage Brokers Association of Ontario (CMBA Ontario) formally opposed the decision. President Jessica Rickerby said affordability was the crisis in hand, not a theoretical future one.

“While inflation is a key concern of Ontarians, so is housing affordability. The difference is that affordability is a pressing issue right now, whereas inflation is – at present – a hypothetical,” Rickerby said.

CMBA Ontario cited approximately 5,300 new home sales in the Greater Toronto Area in 2025, a record low and an 81% fall from normal levels, according to the association.

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.5%, forecasting elevated inflation into 2028 as higher costs keep housing activity weak and push shelter inflation higher.
items.body:
Canada’s central bank raised its key policy rate as it tries to tame rising inflation. The Bank of Canada (BoC) hiked its overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.5% this morning, its first hike in over 3 years. In the accompanying report, the BoC warns of elevated inflation into mid-2028. Higher input and financing costs will also keep housing activity weak while boosting shelter inflation.

Canadian Inflation Isn’t Expected To Return To Target Until 2028

The BoC sees elevated inflation into 2028. The latest forecast from the central bank shows CPI inflation above 3% through Q3 2027. That’s roughly a point higher than they anticipated in their July report. It isn’t expected to return to their 2% target rate until mid-2028. While elevated inflation has largely been confined to energy and related categories, the Bank expects those pressures to spread over the next year.

High energy prices are spreading into production, transportation, and imports. Businesses have absorbed much of the increase so far, but expect to pass more on to consumers over the next 12 months, warns the BoC. Even after energy inflation turns negative in late 2027, earlier cost increases will continue to work their way through supply chains and boost prices.

Source: Bank of Canada.

Canadian Housing Investment Forecast To Lag The Economy

Higher rates are seen putting a drag on one of the country’s biggest components of GDP—housing investment. Residential investment primarily consists of spending on new home construction and substantial renovation. This sector is seen averaging less than 1% growth in 2027 and 2028. In contrast, GDP growth is expected to be roughly 2% for both years. The whole economy isn’t expected to slow, but housing will underperform.

Weak demand and high input costs are the reasons they cite. A lack of affordability, slow population growth, and rising borrowing costs are seen hitting the brakes on the demand side. Meanwhile, higher energy costs and imported input costs will make construction more expensive, throttling building activity.

Weak Housing Activity Isn’t Expected To Slow Rising Shelter Costs

Weak housing investment isn’t expected to slow shelter service inflation. It’s forecast to rise from just over 1% at the end of 2026 to 2% in 2027, and remain near that level into 2028. Higher material, equipment, construction, and maintenance costs are seen as the primary driver. Rising borrowing costs are expected to add further upward pressure. Rent inflation is seen as one of the few moderating factors for shelter, but it only partially offsets the other factors.

The impact on home prices isn’t clear, but higher expenses and weak demand aren’t bullish. At the same time, weak activity doesn’t automatically lead to affordability improvements.

The BoC report leaves an inflationary issue untouched: how government-backed construction spending supports higher input costs. Large projects compete for workers, resources, equipment, and land—even as private housing demand weakens. That spending can limit the disinflationary relief normally associated with a slowdown, leaving input costs elevated despite weak qualified demand.

items.title: Here's what Tiff Macklem said after the BoC's rate hike
items.description: Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response
items.content: <p>Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288017115537128.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response
items.body:
The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, as Governor Tiff Macklem declared the central bank's commitment to price stability in "this period of global upheaval," anchoring the decision in a Middle East oil shock and unsettled Canada-US trade relations.

Speaking alongside Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers in Ottawa, Macklem identified two developments that had shifted the Bank's calculus since July 2026: a deteriorating inflation outlook, with oil prices expected to "remain higher for longer" as the Middle East conflict persisted, and a stronger domestic recovery despite US tariff pressure.

"We are mindful that uncertainty is still elevated," he said.

"Developments in the Middle East and Canada-US trade relations both remain fluid."

Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation has held near 3% since April and is projected to reach roughly 3.5% by year-end, with the 2% target not expected until mid-2028.

CPI excluding gasoline remains at 2.2% and core inflation sits near 2%.

"The longer energy prices remain high, the more likely it is these costs will spill over to consumer prices more broadly," Macklem said.

Oil, trade tensions, and the inflation risk that tipped the Bank's hand

Governing Council weighed that risk against solid economic data. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 3.3% in the second quarter, with preliminary indicators pointing to about 2% growth in the third quarter, per the Bank of Canada's October 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

The unemployment rate has held near 6.5%, and full-year 2026 GDP growth is forecast at just 1% as US tariffs weigh on activity.

Not all forecasters agreed the moment called for action.Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada (NBC) in Montréal, told the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary last week that core data argued for patience.

"Core inflation is still at 2%," he said.

"I don't think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking [on October 28] and if they do hike, they can't be too aggressive."

What the hike means for mortgage brokers

For Canadian mortgage brokers, the decision reshapes client conversations immediately.

Variable-rate mortgage holders will see payments rise as lenders' prime rates move from 4.45% to 4.70%, a shift that renewal discussions and rate-path strategy had been building toward all year, and Wednesday's announcement intensifies the pressure.

Leah Zlatkin, a Toronto-based licensed mortgage broker and expert commentator with LowestRates.ca, said one move is unlikely to be the last.

"If there is a hike, I do think it's going to be a cycle," Zlatkin said.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao, speaking from Toronto, said Macklem had telegraphed the outcome weeks earlier.

"It was Bank of Canada Governor Macklem's remarks a couple of weeks ago that likely tipped the scales towards today's decision to hike," Ercolao said.

"The Bank of Canada said it does not see a clear offramp to the conflict in the Middle East and is increasingly worried about the risks to inflation."

Governing Council signalled caution on what comes next, stopping short of any firm commitment to further action.

"Looking ahead, Governing Council agreed we would take future decisions one meeting at a time," Macklem said.

"There could be a need to raise the policy rate further, but given the uncertainties, we will proceed carefully."

The Bank's next rate decision is set on December 9.
